newsitem.title: USA: Connecticut tops income list, Mississippi at bottom.
newsitem.headline: Connecticut tops income list, Mississippi at bottom.

text.p: The nation's per capita personal income growth last year was the fastest since 1991, the Commerce Department said Tuesday, with Connecticut leading state rankings and Mississippi staying on the bottom rung.
The per capita personal income growth rate increased to 5.3 percent from 3.9 percent in 1994, the department's revised estimates showed.
The income growth rate for 1995 was revised upward from a preliminary estimate of 5.0 percent.

U.S. per capita income was $23,208 in 1995, up from $22,047 in 1994. The 5.3 percent increase was more than double the 2.4 percent rise in prices as measured by the price index for personal consumption expenditures, Commerce said.
Connecticut topped all other states, with per capita income of $31,776, up from $30,054 in 1994. The state has held the No. 1 spot since 1986, a Commerce Department analyst said.

Mississippi, meanwhile, remained at the bottom, with per capita income of $16,683 last year, although it moved up from $15,906 in 1994. The state has held the last spot since at least 1969, which is the furthest back that current rankings can be compared, the analyst said.
Forty states had faster income growth, most due to large increases in dividend, interest, and rental income and in transfer payments, the department said.
Rhode Island had the fastest growth, at 7.3 percent. Seven of the 10 states with the fastest growth rates were on the East Coast, the report said.
In those seven states "substantial earnings increases in services and wholesale trade also contributed to personal income growth," the department said.

The slowest income growth occurred in North Dakota, which registered a 2.3 percent gain last year. Nine of the 11 states with the slowest growth were in the Plains, Rocky Mountain, and Far West regions, the report said.
In most of those 11 states, personal income increased at below-average rates and population either decreased or increased at below-average rates, the department said.
